hook.text: A test can tell you that an effect is there. It can't tell you how big it is.

huge.text: Take two groups of three hundred thousand, on a score that varies by about fifteen points.

p.text: Group B's average is higher by about a seventh of a point. The p-value is under three in ten thousand... highly significant.

tiny.text: But a seventh of a point, against a spread of fifteen, is less than one percent of a standard deviation.

real.text: It's real... and it's far too small to matter.

why.text: With enough data, almost any difference passes a test. So passing stops telling you whether to care.

d-in.text: What you need is a measure of size.

dscene.text: Cohen's d is the gap between two averages, counted in standard deviations.

one.text: It has no units. A d of one means the averages sit one full standard deviation apart.

labels.text: Cohen called zero point two small, zero point five medium, and zero point eight large.

overlap.text: Even large leaves a lot of overlap. At zero point eight, the two curves still share more than two thirds of their area.

stake.text: The labels are only a start. What counts as big depends on what's at stake.

sweep-in.text: And unlike a p-value, a size doesn't depend on how much data you have.

sweep.text: Here the true effect is fixed at zero point three. Now grow the sample, from twenty per group to fifty thousand.

plunge.text: The p-value plunges, from zero point one five to a number so small it prints as zero.

settle.text: But d just settles... near zero point three.

world.text: The effect size is a fact about the world. The p-value is a fact about the world AND your sample.

rates-in.text: When the outcome is yes or no, there are two ways to say the size.

rates.text: Say a new checkout button lifts conversion from three percent to four point two.

relative.text: That's forty percent more... or one point two percentage points.

both.text: The first sounds bigger. Report both, so a reader can judge.

interval.text: And give every effect size an interval. Here, a d of zero point three six, plausibly anywhere from zero point one to zero point six.

trio.text: How big, how precise, and whether it's there at all. Report all three.

part2-in.text: But even a well measured effect can mean something other than it seems.

admit.text: Berkeley's nineteen seventy-three graduate admissions are the famous case. Here's the pattern in two departments.

overall.text: Overall, fifty-five percent of the men get in, and only thirty-three percent of the women.

split.text: Now split by department. In the easy one, women do better, sixty-five percent to sixty.

hard.text: In the hard one, women do better again, twenty-seven and a half to twenty-five.

how.text: Ahead in both departments... and behind overall. How?

mix.text: Six hundred of the seven hundred women applied to the hard one. Six hundred of the men, to the easy one.

name.text: That's Simpson's paradox. A lurking variable, here the department, sat unevenly across the groups.

ask.text: So before you trust a total, ask what it's averaging over.

confound-in.text: And a lurking variable can flip a slope, too.

confound.text: Here's weekly exercise against blood pressure, for a hundred and four people.

rises.text: One line through everyone rises, about nine points for every extra hour of exercise a week.

bands.text: Now color them by age. Inside every age band, the line falls.

age.text: Older people here exercise more, and have higher blood pressure. Age drives both. It's a confounder.

coin.text: The cure is a randomized experiment. If a coin decides who exercises, age can't.

rtm-in.text: Sometimes, though, there's no third variable at all. Just luck.

rtm.text: Five hundred salespeople. Every month, each one's number is their skill, plus luck.

top.text: Take the top tenth in month one. They averaged a hundred and thirty-two.

next-month.text: The same people, the next month... a hundred and thirteen.

bottom.text: The bottom tenth went the other way, from seventy up to ninety-five.

nothing.text: Nobody did anything. Part of every extreme score was luck, and luck doesn't repeat.

coach.text: Coach that bottom group, and they'd improve anyway... and the coaching would get the credit.

control.text: To credit it, you'd need a control group, just as extreme, and left alone.

look-in.text: The next traps come from choosing what you look at.
